title: Musculoskeletal Trauma
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains what happens to bone, ligament, tendon, and muscle after injury. It covers how a fracture heals and why healing stalls, which fractures threaten a blood supply or a nerve, how soft tissue injuries differ, and three complications of crushed or ischemic muscle: compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and myositis ossificans. Board questions usually describe an injury and ask what structure is at risk, what the laboratory or examination finding means, or why a complication appears when it does. Each answer comes from anatomy (where vessels and nerves run), physiology (pressure and perfusion), or cell biology (how tissue repairs).
prerequisites: Bone histology, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and endochondral and intramembranous ossification (MS-1, MS-2)
Dense regular connective tissue and collagen types I, II, and III (MS-6)
Blood supply and nerves of the wrist, elbow, and hip (MS-3, MS-5)
Capillary hydrostatic pressure and fluid exchange across the capillary wall
Acute inflammation and repair by regeneration or scar

connections.how: Myositis ossificans and osteosarcoma both make bone, and the direction of maturation is what separates a reactive lesion from a malignant one.
Osteoporosis sets up hip, wrist, and vertebral fractures, and avascular necrosis of the femoral head leads to secondary osteoarthritis.
Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis causes acute tubular injury through casts, heme toxicity, and vasoconstriction.
Fat embolism is a form of nonthrombotic embolism that can progress to acute respiratory distress.
ATP depletion and calcium overload explain why muscle cells die in crush injury and extreme exertion.

terms.def: The mass of repair tissue (granulation tissue, cartilage, and woven bone) that bridges and splints a healing fracture.
Immature bone with randomly oriented collagen fibers, laid down quickly during repair and later replaced by lamellar bone.
A fracture that heals more slowly than expected for its site and type but is still progressing.
A fracture in which healing has stopped without bony bridging; a nonunion with persistent motion can form a false joint (pseudarthrosis).
Death of bone and marrow from loss of blood supply, also called osteonecrosis.
Respiratory, neurologic, and skin dysfunction 1 to 3 days after fat droplets enter the circulation, usually from long bone fracture.
Stretch or tear of a ligament.
Stretch or tear of a muscle or tendon, most often at the myotendinous junction.
Ischemia of muscle and nerve caused by rising tissue pressure inside a closed fascial compartment.
Permanent flexion deformity of the wrist and fingers after forearm flexor muscle necrosis and fibrosis.
Breakdown of skeletal muscle that releases creatine kinase, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate into the blood.
Formation of mature bone in soft tissue where bone does not normally exist; myositis ossificans is the post-traumatic form in muscle.

sections.title: Fracture healing and why it fails

blocks.text: Bone is one of the few adult tissues that heals by regeneration rather than scar: a well-healed fracture is replaced by true bone and can regain its original strength. Most fractures heal indirectly (secondary healing), repeating the sequence of skeletal development. Only when fragments are fixed rigidly in direct contact does bone heal directly (primary healing), with osteoclasts tunneling across the line and osteoblasts filling the tunnels, and no visible callus.

Secondary healing starts when torn vessels in the bone, marrow, and periosteum bleed into the gap. The clot is a fibrin scaffold, and platelets and macrophages release growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, and bone morphogenetic proteins, BMPs) that recruit mesenchymal progenitor cells from the inner (cambium) layer of the periosteum and the marrow. Bone at the fracture ends loses its supply and dies back a short distance, and osteoclasts remove it. Within the gap, oxygen is low and the fragments move slightly, conditions that push progenitors to become chondrocytes, so the gap fills with granulation tissue and fibrocartilage (soft callus). Under the periosteum away from the gap, where oxygen is better, osteoblasts form woven bone directly by intramembranous ossification. As capillaries invade the soft callus, cartilage calcifies and is replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification (hard callus), and the fracture becomes clinically stable. Remodeling then replaces woven with lamellar bone, removes excess callus, and aligns trabeculae with the loads the bone carries.

blocks.title: Secondary fracture healing
steps: Torn vessels form hematoma; fibrin scaffold and growth factors
Inflammation; dead bone ends resorbed by osteoclasts
Progenitors form granulation tissue and fibrocartilage (soft callus)
Vessels invade; cartilage replaced by woven bone (hard callus)
Woven bone remodeled to lamellar bone along stress lines
blocks.caption: Approximate timing: hematoma and inflammation in the first days to a week, soft callus by about 1 to 3 weeks, hard callus over weeks to about 3 months, remodeling over months to years.

blocks.text: Every stage depends on new blood vessels and on the right amount of motion. Delayed union means healing is slower than expected; nonunion means it has stopped. Two patterns explain the causes. With too much motion and good biology, cartilage and fibrous tissue keep forming but never ossify, producing abundant callus that does not bridge (hypertrophic nonunion). With poor biology, little callus forms at all (atrophic nonunion).

blocks.title: Factors that delay union
rows: Few vessels reach the gap, so soft callus cannot be converted to bone; worst in bones with a single or retrograde supply and with periosteal stripping
Excess motion tears ingrowing capillaries and keeps the gap fibrous or cartilaginous
Bacteria and neutrophil enzymes destroy matrix; dead bone (sequestrum) cannot be revascularized
Nicotine constricts vessels and inhibits osteoblasts; carbon monoxide lowers oxygen delivery
Microvascular disease, impaired angiogenesis, advanced glycation end products, and weaker osteoblast function
Too little protein for matrix, vitamin C for collagen hydroxylation, or calcium and vitamin D for mineralization
blocks.caption: Glucocorticoid excess and advanced age slow healing by similar effects on progenitor cells and blood flow.

blocks.text: The complication of a fracture follows from what lies next to the bone and how blood enters it. Avascular necrosis threatens any fragment whose vessels enter from the other side of the fracture line; nerve and artery injury threatens structures lying directly against a displaced fragment.

The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually after a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist extended. Branches of the radial artery enter at the waist and distal pole, and the proximal pole receives its blood by retrograde flow through the bone. A waist fracture therefore cuts off the proximal pole, which can die and fail to unite. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the key sign, and the first radiograph may be normal because an undisplaced crack becomes visible only after bone along the fracture margins is resorbed.

The adult femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular arteries, branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that run up the femoral neck inside the joint capsule. A displaced intracapsular (femoral neck) fracture tears them, so the head may necrose and later collapse. The artery of the ligament of the head contributes little in adults. Extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures leave the retinacular vessels intact and rarely cause necrosis.

The supracondylar humerus fracture is the classic elbow fracture of children, typically about 5 to 7 years old, after a fall on an outstretched arm. In the usual extension type the distal fragment shifts posteriorly and the sharp proximal fragment is driven forward into the brachial artery and median nerve, which lie in front of the distal humerus on the brachialis. The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve is often affected, weakening flexion of the thumb and index fingertip. Arterial injury and swelling can cause forearm compartment syndrome (C04). With medial displacement of the distal fragment the radial nerve is at risk, and the uncommon flexion type endangers the ulnar nerve.

blocks.title: Fracture, structure at risk, and result
rows: Retinacular branches of medial circumflex femoral artery
Brachial artery, median and anterior interosseous nerves
Hand ischemia, nerve palsy, compartment syndrome
blocks.caption: Anatomy predicts the complication: retrograde or capsular blood supply, and neurovascular structures adjacent to the fragment.

blocks.text: Fat droplets enter the circulation in most patients with long bone or pelvic fractures because marrow fat is forced into torn venules held open by rigid bone. Only a small proportion develop fat embolism syndrome, and the 1 to 3 day delay reflects its second, biochemical stage: lipase breaks fat into free fatty acids that injure endothelium, and platelets aggregate on the droplets. Pulmonary capillary injury causes hypoxemia and can progress to acute respiratory distress. Deformable droplets pass the lung or a patent foramen ovale to reach the brain (confusion) and skin, where petechiae over the chest, axillae, and conjunctivae reflect capillary damage and thrombocytopenia.

blocks.title: Fat embolism syndrome
steps: Long bone fracture forces marrow fat into torn veins
Droplets lodge in pulmonary capillaries
Lipase releases free fatty acids; platelets aggregate
Endothelial injury: hypoxemia, possible respiratory distress
Systemic droplets: confusion and petechiae, 1 to 3 days after injury
blocks.caption: Mechanical lodging is immediate; the toxic free fatty acid stage explains the delay before symptoms.

blocks.predict: An 80-year-old woman with an intertrochanteric fracture and a 78-year-old woman with a displaced subcapital femoral neck fracture both heal their fractures. Which is more likely to develop femoral head collapse a year later?
blocks.explain: The femoral neck fracture, because it lies inside the capsule and tears the retinacular arteries that supply the head; the intertrochanteric fracture is distal to them.

blocks.text: Soft tissue injuries are named by the tissue that fails. A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament, which joins bone to bone; it is graded from microscopic fiber tearing with a stable joint (grade I) through partial tear (grade II) to complete rupture with instability (grade III). A strain is a stretch or tear of muscle or tendon. It usually occurs at the myotendinous junction, the weakest link, during eccentric contraction (the muscle lengthening while contracting), so muscles crossing two joints, such as the hamstrings, are most often affected.

A contusion is a bruise: a blunt blow crushes tissue without breaking the skin, and blood from ruptured capillaries spreads into it. The color change of a bruise follows heme breakdown by macrophages: red-purple hemoglobin, then green biliverdin made by heme oxygenase, then yellow bilirubin and brown hemosiderin. A dislocation is complete loss of contact between articular surfaces, whereas a subluxation is partial loss. Because capsule and ligaments must tear to allow it, a dislocation can stretch nearby nerves and vessels, as with the axillary nerve in anterior shoulder dislocation.

blocks.title: Soft tissue injuries compared
rows: Joint forced beyond its range (ankle inversion)
Joint pain and swelling; laxity if severe
Pain on active contraction and on stretch
Force driving the joint past its restraints
Deformity and loss of motion; risk to nearby nerves and vessels
blocks.caption: Name the tissue that failed, then predict the finding.

blocks.text: Ligaments and tendons are dense regular connective tissue: parallel bundles of type I collagen with few fibroblasts, little blood flow, and a low metabolic rate. After a tear, healing passes through inflammation, a proliferative phase in which fibroblasts lay down disorganized type III collagen, and a long remodeling phase. The repair tissue has thinner fibrils, more type III collagen, and fewer mature cross-links, so it stays weaker and more lax than the original for a year or more, which explains recurrent sprains and chronic instability. Intra-articular ligaments heal worst: synovial fluid dilutes and breaks down the clot that should form a scaffold, and the torn ends retract, which is why a torn anterior cruciate ligament does not heal on its own while the extra-articular medial collateral ligament usually does. Muscle heals better because satellite cells beneath the basal lamina can regenerate fibers, although a large tear still leaves scar.

sections.title: Compartment syndrome and Volkmann ischemic contracture

blocks.text: Muscles of the limbs lie in compartments bounded by bone and deep fascia, which barely stretches. Any added volume inside a compartment therefore raises its pressure steeply. Normal resting compartment pressure is about 0 to 8 mmHg. Volume rises from bleeding after a fracture (most often the tibia, then the forearm), swelling after crush injury, edema when blood flow returns after a period of ischemia (reperfusion), or external restriction by a tight cast or circumferential burn eschar.

Tissue pressure opposes the pressure inside thin-walled vessels. Veins and capillaries collapse first because their pressures are lowest, so venous outflow and capillary perfusion fail while the higher arterial pressure still drives a pulse through the compartment. Ischemic capillaries leak more fluid, which raises compartment pressure further and closes the cycle. Perfusion of a compartment depends on the difference between arterial pressure and compartment pressure, so hypotension lowers the compartment pressure at which ischemia begins.

blocks.title: The pressure cycle in compartment syndrome
steps: Bleeding or edema adds volume to a closed compartment
Compartment pressure exceeds venous and capillary pressure
Muscle and nerve become ischemic
Ischemic capillaries leak more fluid
Added fluid raises compartment pressure further
blocks.caption: The loop is self-sustaining: each turn raises pressure further.

blocks.text: The findings follow the order in which tissues fail. Ischemic muscle is intensely painful, so the earliest sign is pain out of proportion to the injury. Passively stretching the muscles of the compartment (for example, extending the toes for the deep posterior leg) lengthens ischemic fibers and raises pressure, sharply worsening the pain. Nerves then lose function, causing paresthesia, starting with the nerve that runs through the compartment, such as numbness of the first web space from the deep fibular nerve in the anterior leg. Paralysis comes later. Pallor and pulselessness appear late or not at all, so a palpable pulse does not exclude the diagnosis. Nerve conduction fails within about an hour, and muscle necrosis becomes irreversible after about 6 hours of ischemia. Dead muscle can release myoglobin and potassium, linking this condition to rhabdomyolysis (C05).

blocks.title: Why the pulse persists
blocks.text: A man with a tibial shaft fracture has a compartment pressure of 45 mmHg and blood pressure 120/70 mmHg. Capillary pressure is roughly 10 to 30 mmHg, highest at the arterial end, so a tissue pressure of 45 mmHg collapses capillaries and venules and stops nutrient flow. Arterial pressure (70 to 120 mmHg) still exceeds 45 mmHg, so the artery stays open and the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. The difference between diastolic and compartment pressure is 70 minus 45, or 25 mmHg; a difference of about 30 mmHg or less is commonly taken to mean inadequate perfusion. If his blood pressure fell to 90/50 mmHg, the difference would shrink to 5 mmHg, and ischemia would worsen without any change in compartment pressure.

Volkmann ischemic contracture is the late result of untreated forearm compartment syndrome, classically after a supracondylar humerus fracture. The deep flexors of the volar compartment (flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus) are most vulnerable because they lie deepest, against bone. Necrotic muscle is replaced by fibrous tissue that shortens, producing a flexed wrist, flexed finger joints (often with extended metacarpophalangeal joints), and a pronated forearm, with sensory loss from median and ulnar nerve ischemia. Unlike Dupuytren contracture (MS-13-E), the problem lies in dead muscle rather than in the palmar fascia.

blocks.predict: A patient with a forearm fracture in a cast has severe pain on passive finger extension, a normal radial pulse, and normal capillary refill. Is compartment syndrome excluded?
blocks.explain: No. Arterial pressure stays above compartment pressure until late, so the pulse persists while capillary perfusion to muscle has already failed. Pain with passive stretch is the earliest reliable sign.

blocks.text: Rhabdomyolysis is breakdown of skeletal muscle with release of its contents into the blood. The common pathway is ATP depletion or direct membrane damage. Without ATP the Na+/K+-ATPase and the Ca2+ pumps fail, cytosolic calcium rises, and calcium activates proteases and phospholipases, sustains contraction, and damages mitochondria, so the cell breaks down. Causes include crush injury and prolonged immobilization on a hard surface, extreme exertion (especially in heat, with hypokalemia, or with sickle cell trait), seizures, alcohol and cocaine, metabolic myopathies such as McArdle disease, and statins, whose muscle toxicity is thought to involve reduced coenzyme Q10 and protein prenylation and rises when a second drug slows statin clearance.

blocks.title: From muscle injury to acute kidney injury
steps: Crush, exertion, or toxin depletes muscle ATP or tears the sarcolemma
Cytosolic calcium rises; proteases and phospholipases destroy the cell
CK, myoglobin, potassium, phosphate, and urate enter the blood
Fluid sequestered in swollen muscle lowers renal perfusion
Filtered myoglobin forms casts and its heme injures tubules
Acute kidney injury with hyperkalemia and acidosis
blocks.caption: Kidney injury combines renal hypoperfusion, tubular obstruction, and direct heme toxicity.

blocks.text: Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive marker. Rhabdomyolysis is usually defined as CK above about 5 times the upper reference limit, and values in the tens of thousands of U/L are common. CK peaks at about 1 to 3 days and falls slowly, whereas myoglobin, a small 17 kDa protein, is filtered and cleared within hours, so myoglobinuria may already have cleared when CK is still very high.

The urine dipstick detects the peroxidase-like activity of heme, and it cannot tell intact red cells from free heme protein. A strongly positive blood reaction with few or no red cells on microscopy therefore means myoglobin or free hemoglobin, and the urine is often red-brown or tea-colored. In the kidney, myoglobin precipitates with uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) in acidic tubular fluid to form pigmented casts, its heme iron drives oxidative injury to tubular cells, and free heme scavenges nitric oxide, constricting renal vessels.

blocks.title: Expected laboratory pattern
rows: Dipstick positive for blood, few red cells
Filtered myoglobin has heme peroxidase activity
Potassium released from muscle, worsened by kidney injury; can cause arrhythmia
Phosphate and purines released from muscle
Calcium deposits in necrotic muscle, then is released during recovery
Organic acids from muscle and reduced renal acid excretion
Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts
blocks.caption: Hemolysis also gives a heme-positive dipstick without red cells, but CK is normal and plasma may be pink.

blocks.title: Myoglobin or hemoglobin?
blocks.text: Two patients have urine dipsticks 3+ for blood and 0 to 2 red cells per high-power field. Patient A ran a marathon in heat: CK 48,000 U/L, potassium 6.2 mmol/L, plasma clear. Patient B has a mechanical heart valve: CK normal, LDH high, haptoglobin low, plasma pink. In both, free heme pigment explains the dipstick. In A, myoglobin is small and loosely bound in plasma, so it is filtered and cleared quickly and plasma stays clear, while CK confirms muscle as the source. In B, free hemoglobin first saturates haptoglobin and stays in plasma, coloring it pink, and the low haptoglobin and high LDH point to red cell destruction.

sections.title: Myositis ossificans and its distinction from osteosarcoma

blocks.text: Myositis ossificans is a reactive, benign formation of bone within skeletal muscle or nearby soft tissue. It typically follows a contusion or repeated injury in an athletic adolescent or young adult, most often in the quadriceps or the brachialis, although some patients recall no injury. Injured muscle releases inflammatory signals and bone morphogenetic proteins that drive local mesenchymal progenitor cells to become osteoblasts, so bone forms where muscle healed with hemorrhage and granulation tissue.

The lesion evolves predictably. In the first weeks it is a painful, enlarging soft tissue mass. Faint mineralization appears after about 3 to 4 weeks, and by about 6 to 8 weeks imaging shows a well-defined peripheral rim of bone. Over months the mass matures, often shrinks, and becomes painless. It is usually separated from the adjacent cortex by a thin lucent cleft.

The key feature is zonation. The center contains loosely arranged, proliferating fibroblasts that can show mitoses; the middle zone holds osteoid and woven bone rimmed by osteoblasts; and the periphery is mature lamellar bone. The lesion matures from the outside in. Osteosarcoma shows the reverse: malignant cells with marked atypia and atypical mitoses lay down lace-like osteoid directly, the most immature and atypical tissue lies at the expanding edge, and that edge infiltrates and destroys surrounding bone and muscle, often lifting the periosteum. An early biopsy of myositis ossificans that samples only the cellular center can look alarming, so the pattern across the whole lesion is what matters.

blocks.title: Myositis ossificans versus osteosarcoma
rows: Immature center, mature bone at periphery
Most immature, atypical tissue at periphery
Well defined; lucent cleft from cortex
Infiltrative; arises from and destroys bone
Matures and often shrinks over months
blocks.caption: Direction of maturation separates a reactive lesion from a malignant one.

blocks.text: Post-traumatic myositis ossificans should not be confused with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, a rare autosomal dominant disease caused by an activating mutation in ACVR1, a BMP type I receptor. In that disease, minor injury triggers progressive ossification of muscles, tendons, and ligaments throughout the body, often with malformed great toes from birth. Heterotopic ossification in general also follows hip surgery, spinal cord injury, and burns.

blocks.predict: A biopsy from a thigh mass in a 17-year-old soccer player shows proliferating fibroblasts with mitoses in the center and mature trabecular bone around the edge. Is this more consistent with osteosarcoma or myositis ossificans?
blocks.explain: Myositis ossificans, because its most mature bone lies at the periphery around an immature center; osteosarcoma has its least mature, most atypical tissue at the infiltrating edge.

integration.text: Anatomy predicts most fracture complications. The scaphoid and the femoral head share a blood supply that reaches them from one direction, so a fracture across that path causes avascular necrosis, and the supracondylar humerus lies directly behind the brachial artery and median nerve. Physiology explains compartment syndrome: capillaries fail before arteries because their pressure is lower, which is why pain and passive-stretch pain come before loss of pulses. Biochemistry and renal pathology link crushed muscle to the kidney through ATP depletion, calcium overload, myoglobin casts, and heme toxicity, and the urine dipstick reads heme, not red cells.

Repair biology connects the rest. Bone regenerates by repeating endochondral and intramembranous ossification, provided blood vessels and limited motion allow it; ligaments heal slowly with weaker type III collagen scar; and injured muscle can either regenerate from satellite cells, scar and contract after ischemia, or ossify. Timings and pressure thresholds in this chapter are approximate and vary with the patient and the source, so they support reasoning rather than replace the whole clinical picture.

summary: Secondary fracture healing runs from hematoma and inflammation to soft callus, hard callus by endochondral ossification, and remodeling to lamellar bone.
Healing needs blood vessels and limited motion; poor supply, instability, infection, smoking, diabetes, and malnutrition cause delayed union or nonunion.
Scaphoid waist and displaced femoral neck fractures cut a one-directional blood supply, causing avascular necrosis of the proximal pole or femoral head.
Extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures injure the brachial artery and median (anterior interosseous) nerve and can cause forearm compartment syndrome.
Fat embolism syndrome appears 1 to 3 days after long bone fracture as hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae, from free fatty acid injury to endothelium.

Sprain is ligament, strain is muscle or tendon, contusion is bleeding from a blow, and dislocation is loss of joint contact; ligaments heal slowly because they are hypocellular and poorly vascularized.
In compartment syndrome capillaries collapse before arteries, so pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch precede loss of pulses; Volkmann contracture is the late forearm result.
Rhabdomyolysis gives very high CK, a heme-positive dipstick without red cells, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, early hypocalcemia, and acute kidney injury.
Myositis ossificans matures from the periphery inward, leaving a shell of mature bone around an immature center; osteosarcoma has its most atypical tissue at the infiltrating edge.

verify: Stage timings for fracture healing (soft callus by about 1 to 3 weeks, hard callus to about 3 months) vary between sources and by bone and age; values are stated as approximate.
Definitions of delayed union and nonunion (time since injury and time without radiographic progress) differ among sources; confirm whether NABNE expects a specific time cutoff.

Compartment syndrome thresholds (diastolic minus compartment pressure of about 30 mmHg or less, or an absolute pressure above about 30 mmHg) and ischemia times (nerve dysfunction within about an hour, irreversible muscle necrosis after about 6 hours) vary between sources.
Nerve most often injured in supracondylar humerus fractures (anterior interosseous versus radial) differs between orthopedic series; confirm the answer NABNE expects.
The CK threshold for rhabdomyolysis (about 5 times the upper reference limit, often quoted as above about 1,000 U/L) and the CK level that predicts kidney injury vary between sources.

The mechanism of statin myopathy (coenzyme Q10 depletion, reduced prenylation, and a rare anti-HMG-CoA reductase immune-mediated form) is not fully settled; it is presented as the leading explanation.
Timing of mineralization in myositis ossificans (faint at about 3 to 4 weeks, peripheral rim by about 6 to 8 weeks) and the proportion of cases without known trauma vary between sources.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponym Volkmann and the six Ps of acute ischemia, or only the descriptive findings.
